newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Base metals volatile after early peaks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Base metals volatile after early peaks.

text.p: Base metals stole the focus from other commodities on Tuesday as zinc, aluminium, copper and nickel shot up but then struggled to hold gains.
Zinc showed the most stamina, extending Monday's gains to reach a 4-1/2 year high above $1,250 per tonne on the London metal Exchange (LME).
It was helped up by a fall of 1,400 tonnes in LME-supervised warehouse stocks and later in the day resisted a wave of profit-taking that swept the London metals market.

But the profit taking completely eroded strong gains in aluminium which had jumped to a 14-month high above $1,700 per tonne amid concern over Russian supply. It ended the London day at $1,685, down $5 from Monday.
Traders had acted on fears that Russian exports were under threat from calls to curb foreign ownership of the domestic industry.
"Potentially, it's a worrying situation," said Martin Squires, analyst at LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co. "It helped the market firm up in combination with the general market feeling."
Copper failed to hold on to a nine-month high of $2,420 reached in morning trade, slipping lower before ending at $2,395 per tonne.
Nickel, meanwhile, tumbled below the $8,300 level as fears of a strike at Russia's Arctic metals complex at Norilsk eased.

Workers at Norilsk, which supplies almost a quarter of the world's nickel, have threatened to strike over pay and holiday arrears, but a trade union spokesman on Tuesday discounted the possibility of major disruptions to output.
Angus MacMillan, analyst at Billiton Metals said: "I'd be very surprised if the union called an all-out strike. It would be a case of cutting off its nose to spite its face."
But he added that noone would go short of nickel while the threat of a strike rumbled on.
Brokers GNI said in a market commentary: "there is no reason not to plump for a global boom (in base metals) at some stage in the next few months."
A report by technical analysts Wavetrack said zinc could surpass a medium-term target of $1,550 by early 1998. It also predicted a bull market in nickel.
Coffee prices -up around 50 percent this year- stayed strong with a new rally in New York led by fund buying.
London robusta futures made a sluggish start and were dogged by overhead scale-up hedge selling and expectations that a rally in New York has run its course, traders said.
In fact, contract highs were reached in New York, with benchmark arabica May futures hitting 196.00 cents/lb before profit taking by locals and commission houses.

London tracked New York up and robusta futures for May reached $1,698 per tonne, up from $1,655 on Monday. Technical analysts said they saw them going even higher to challenge a February peak of $1,720.
"From a fundamental point of view, this market should come down soon, but so far it is shrugging off negative news as if it were a bothersome irrelevance," said brokers GNI in a report.

Coffee's rally this year was underpinned by supply concerns. Recent gains were fuelled by unrest among Brazilian port workers who were to meet with port operators on Tuesday to try and avert a threatened strike on Wednesday.

With traders awaiting news of an agreement from the meeting, the threat of a strike also held up soybean and wheat prices. Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were up slightly at $3.75 a bushel towards mid-session.
Soybean futures, which opened around two cents higher, were also supported by worries of a slowdown in Brazil's soybean harvest due to rainy weather.

Cocoa extended an advance to reach session highs in London and dealers said it was heading for further gains. But white sugar futures drifted lower with minimal trading volume reported, while precious metals also traded in narrow ranges.
Crude oil was slightly firmer after it extended a recent decline on Monday, with London April futures for the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend just above $19 per barrel after $18.75 on Monday.
The oil market awaited weekly demand and supply data from the American Petroleum Institute.
